narrative:
The model estimated a 76.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your admission application was denied because that risk was judged too high. This is a statistical forecast, not a certainty, but it means the decision was driven mainly by patterns associated with bar failure.

The strongest influence was your third-year academic standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. The second-strongest signal was your first-year standing, where you were in the second-lowest decile compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile; this also pushed toward failure, though less strongly. Your LSAT score of 29.50, below the accepted average of 37.18, actually worked in the opposite direction—it was the third most important factor and pushed somewhat toward passing—but it was not enough to offset the academic-standing signals.

To move forward, request a human review and explain any context behind your early grades. Ask what threshold or supplemental evidence can support reconsideration, consider retaking the LSAT, and discuss a plan for strengthening your academic record before reapplying. Use this as a planning signal, not a final judgment.
